title: HOW THE REAL ROVERS STUDIED ROCKS

sub.text: Spirit and Opportunity did NOT bring samples home: they studied each rock right where they found it.

slides.title: SPOT FROM AFAR
slides.text: Pancam is a pair of color cameras on the rover's mast, at about the height of a person's eyes. Its pictures let scientists see the terrain in 3D. Mini-TES measured the infrared (heat) light given off by rocks: every mineral glows in its own pattern, like a fingerprint, so the team could tell from far away which rocks were worth a visit.
slides.why: The rovers moved slowly, so the team had to choose each target carefully before spending days driving to it.
slides.mentor: Let's see how the real rovers studied rocks, one step at a time.

slides.title: DRIVE CLOSER
slides.text: Mars is so far away that a radio command takes several minutes to arrive, so nobody could drive the rover live with a joystick. The team planned the commands and sent them; the rover then drove on its own, using its hazard cameras (Hazcams) to detect and avoid obstacles.
slides.why: Driving was slow and risky. Picking the wrong rock could waste days of a mission that was planned to last only 90 sols.

slides.title: LOOK UP CLOSE
slides.text: The Microscopic Imager sits at the end of the robotic arm. It took extreme close-up black-and-white pictures of rocks and soils. The size, shape and layering of the grains are clues about the processes that formed the rock.
slides.why: The texture of a rock tells HOW it formed, not only WHAT it is made of.

slides.title: GRIND THE SURFACE
slides.text: The outside of a Martian rock is covered by dust and a weathered surface that hides what the rock is really made of. The Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT) used rotating grinding teeth to gnaw into the rock and reveal fresh mineral surfaces.
slides.why: It is like cutting an apple in half: you only learn what is inside after you remove the skin.

slides.title: MEASURE
slides.text: APXS was placed on the fresh surface to measure which chemical elements the rock contains. The Mössbauer spectrometer identified iron-bearing minerals. At Meridiani, Opportunity found hematite and jarosite, a mineral that forms in acidic water.
slides.why: Some minerals only form in water, so finding them is strong evidence that Mars was wet in the past.

slides.title: SEND IT HOME
slides.text: The rovers sent their data to Earth, directly or relayed through orbiters like Mars Odyssey, and NASA's Deep Space Network antennas received it. Scientists then compared photos, textures, chemistry and minerals together. By studying the rock record, they confirmed that water was long-standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
slides.why: This is why each rover carried a whole team of instruments, not just one.

real.title: REAL DISCOVERY
real.text: At Meridiani Planum, Opportunity found tiny hematite spheres ("blueberries"); hematite typically forms in water.
